title: 13 — Contracts, Lineage and Observability
html:
13 — Contracts, Lineage and Observability

The one idea: a contract says what a table promises (shape, meaning, quality, freshness, owner). Lineage says where every column came from. Observability checks, continuously, that the promise is being kept. Write all three as data in open formats, so tools can check them and people can query them.

1. What it is

Practice Open standard or tool Question it answers
Data contract ODCS (Open Data Contract Standard) v3.1.0, from the Bitol project (Linux Foundation) What does this dataset promise, and who owns it?
Lineage OpenLineage (open event spec), Unity Catalog lineage and system tables Which job read what and wrote what, column by column?
Observability Databricks data quality monitoring (anomaly detection and data profiling, formerly Lakehouse Monitoring), plus your own checks Is the table fresh, complete and normal today?

The orchestration and governance chapter introduces contracts and observability. This chapter covers the current standards and how to wire them together.

2. Why it matters

  • A renamed column should break a build, not a client report.
  • When a number is wrong, lineage tells you in minutes which upstream table and job to look at.
  • Silent staleness is the most common failure. A monitor that learns each table's normal rhythm catches it.

3. The main ideas

3.1 ODCS v3.1.0

Per the Bitol announcement (December 2025), v3.1.0 adds:

  • relationships between properties,
  • stricter JSON Schema validation,
  • richer metadata,
  • executable SLAs and improved referencing,
  • removal of unused elements.

Every v3.0 contract stays valid. A contract covers the dataset's schema, quality rules (accuracy, completeness, validity), service levels, stakeholders, pricing and infrastructure. Validation tools check that a contract is well formed. They do not run the quality checks against data. Your pipeline or quality tool does that.

# Illustrative ODCS-style contract. Check field names against the v3.1.0 JSON schema before use.
apiVersion: v3.1.0
kind: DataContract
id: fund-nav-daily
name: fund_nav_daily
version: 1.2.0
status: active
schema:
  - name: fund_nav_daily
    properties:
      - name: isin
        logicalType: string
        required: true
        primaryKey: true
      - name: nav_date
        logicalType: date
        required: true
      - name: nav
        logicalType: number
        required: true
        quality:
          - type: sql
            description: NAV must be positive
            query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fund_nav_daily WHERE nav <= 0
            mustBe: 0
slaProperties:
  - property: frequency
    value: 1
    unit: d
team:
  - username: data.owner@example.com
    role: owner

3.2 OpenLineage

An OpenLineage RunEvent has an eventType (START, COMPLETE, FAIL and others), an eventTime, a run (with runId), a job (namespace and name), and inputs and outputs datasets. Facets attach extra detail. The column lineage facet maps each output column to its input fields. Spark, Airflow, dbt and others can emit these events automatically. Marquez is the reference backend.

Inside Databricks, Unity Catalog captures table and column lineage on its own (system.access.table_lineage and column_lineage, see 05). OpenLineage matters for jobs that run outside Databricks, or for a cross-platform view.

3.3 Data quality monitoring on Databricks

Status, checked 2026-10-26: Databricks' product page describes Data Quality Monitoring as including anomaly detection and data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring). One docs page uses the names the other way round, so check the current docs.

  • Anomaly detection evaluates freshness and completeness per table, learning each table's update pattern. It was labelled Beta in some docs, and its alerts entered Beta in March 2026.
  • Table health indicators in Catalog Explorer entered Public Preview in March 2026.
  • Data profiling computes statistics and drift over time into metric tables.
---
title: Contract, lineage and monitoring around one table
---
flowchart LR
    C["ODCS contract (in Git)<br/>schema, rules, SLA, owner"] --> CI["CI: contract test<br/>schema matches, rules compile"]
    CI --> J["Pipeline run"]
    J --> T["silver.fund_nav"]
    J -- "RunEvent with column lineage" --> L["Lineage store<br/>(UC system tables / OpenLineage backend)"]
    T --> M["Monitor<br/>freshness, completeness, drift"]
    M -- "breach" --> X["Exception to table owner"]
    C -. "owner and SLA" .-> M

4. Working code

The script builds an OpenLineage-shaped event and answers "where does this column come from?". It then learns a table's normal gap between commits and flags a late table. Standard library only.

import json, statistics
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# 1. A lineage event shaped like OpenLineage's RunEvent: who ran, what it read, what it wrote,
#    and which output column came from which input columns. Field names follow the public spec's
#    main keys. Facet details are simplified here, so check the spec before emitting real events.
event = {
    "eventType": "COMPLETE",
    "eventTime": "2026-10-23T18:12:04Z",
    "run": {"runId": "0192f3a1-7c2e-7d10-9c51-3f0a1b2c3d4e"},
    "job": {"namespace": "engine", "name": "silver_fund_nav_build"},
    "inputs": [{"namespace": "lake", "name": "bronze.nav_raw"}, {"namespace": "lake", "name": "ref.fund_master"}],
    "outputs": [{"namespace": "lake", "name": "silver.fund_nav", "facets": {"columnLineage": {"fields": {
        "nav":  {"inputFields": [{"namespace": "lake", "name": "bronze.nav_raw", "field": "net_asset_value"}]},
        "isin": {"inputFields": [{"namespace": "lake", "name": "ref.fund_master", "field": "isin"},
                                 {"namespace": "lake", "name": "bronze.nav_raw", "field": "scheme_code"}]}}}}}],
}
def upstream_of(column):
    out = event["outputs"][0]["facets"]["columnLineage"]["fields"][column]["inputFields"]
    return [f"{f['name']}.{f['field']}" for f in out]
print("silver.fund_nav.isin comes from:", upstream_of("isin"))

# 2. Freshness check learned from history: expect the next commit around the usual gap, alert when late.
commits = [datetime(2026, 10, d, 18, 10) + timedelta(minutes=m) for d, m in
           [(14, 0), (15, 4), (16, -3), (19, 2), (20, 1), (21, 5), (22, -2)]]   # business days, Wed 14 Oct to Thu 22 Oct
gaps = [(b - a).total_seconds() / 3600 for a, b in zip(commits, commits[1:]) if (b - a).days < 2]
typical, spread = statistics.median(gaps), statistics.pstdev(gaps)
def check(now):
    hours = (now - commits[-1]).total_seconds() / 3600
    limit = typical + 3 * spread + 1     # one hour of slack. A real monitor also skips weekends and holidays
    return f"{hours:.1f}h since last commit, limit {limit:.1f}h -> " + ("LATE" if hours > limit else "fresh")
print("Typical gap between commits:", round(typical, 2), "hours")
print("Fri 2026-10-23 17:00:", check(datetime(2026, 10, 23, 17, 0)))
print("Fri 2026-10-23 21:30:", check(datetime(2026, 10, 23, 21, 30)))

Output:

silver.fund_nav.isin comes from: ['ref.fund_master.isin', 'bronze.nav_raw.scheme_code']
Typical gap between commits: 23.98 hours
Fri 2026-10-23 17:00: 22.9h since last commit, limit 25.2h -> fresh
Fri 2026-10-23 21:30: 27.4h since last commit, limit 25.2h -> LATE

What to notice:

  • isin in Silver depends on two inputs: the fund master and the raw scheme code. A broken master would break isin even if the raw file is fine.
  • The table normally commits every 24 hours. At 22.9 hours it is fresh, and at 27.4 hours it is late. No fixed threshold was written by hand.
  • The toy model ignores weekends and holidays, so the history ends on a Thursday and the check runs on a Friday. A real monitor uses the business calendar.

5. Common mistakes

  1. A contract in a wiki. Nobody tests it. Keep it as YAML in Git, and test it in CI.
  2. Contracts without owners. Breaches then reach nobody. Put the owner in the contract and route alerts from it.
  3. Lineage only at table level. Column lineage is what finds the cause of one wrong number.
  4. Fixed freshness thresholds for every table. Learn each table's rhythm, or set the SLA per contract.
  5. Monitoring Gold only. Problems start upstream. Monitor Bronze arrival and Silver completeness too.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Write an ODCS contract for a holdings table with three quality rules and a weekly SLA, then validate it with the official JSON schema if you can install the tools.
  2. Extend the script: emit START and COMPLETE events for a run, and compute the run's duration from them.
  3. Add a completeness check: alert if today's row count is below 80% of the median of the last 10 runs.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does an ODCS validator check, and what does it not check?
  2. Name the main parts of an OpenLineage RunEvent.
  3. Why is column lineage more useful than table lineage for incident work?
  4. What two things does Databricks anomaly detection evaluate per table?
  5. Where should a contract live, and when is it tested?

Answers

  1. It checks that the contract is well formed and matches the schema. It doesn't run the quality checks against data.
  2. eventType, eventTime, run, job, inputs, outputs, plus facets.
  3. It narrows a wrong value down to the exact source fields and transformations that produced it.
  4. Freshness and completeness.
  5. In Git, next to the pipeline. It is tested in CI on every change, and its rules run in the pipeline on every load.
